summary: For ages 12–13, this topic is the drawing-accuracy craft of constructing optical ray diagrams: plane-mirror reflection (incident ray, normal, reflected ray with measured angle of reflection equal to angle of incidence, and a dashed virtual image behind the mirror located where two reflected rays' back-extensions meet), refraction through a rectangular glass block (an oblique ray bends toward the normal on entering the glass and away from it on leaving; a ray along the normal does not bend), and a convex-lens principal-ray construction that locates an image and names it real or virtual. The central disciplines are: draw the dashed normal first (perpendicular at the point of incidence) and measure every angle from the normal, never from the surface; use conventions deliberately (ruled straight rays with arrowheads, solid for real light paths, dashed for the normal and virtual/construction extensions); and use two rays to locate an image point. The authentic task is hand-drawing with a physical protractor and ruler on paper with teacher feedback; a guided on-screen construction editor is a strong stand-in for the concepts but does not fully replicate the paper-and-protractor motor skill.
misconceptions: Measuring angles from the mirror/surface instead of from the NORMAL — the signature drawing error; produces a reflected ray at the wrong angle.
Omitting the normal altogether, or drawing it not perpendicular / not at the point of incidence.
Drawing rays freehand or curved instead of ruled straight lines, and leaving off arrowheads so direction of travel is lost.
Using a SOLID line for the virtual image's back-extension (it should be DASHED) — conflating a real light path with a construction line.
Refraction drawn the wrong way — bending away from the normal when entering glass, or drawing a curved path rather than a sharp change of direction exactly at the boundary.
Eyeballing 'equal angles' instead of measuring, so the reflected ray is visibly unequal; sloppy scale/ruler work.
Not knowing which or how many rays to draw — thinking one ray suffices, or picking rays that don't locate the image.
Carrying over the real/virtual confusion — drawing the plane-mirror image as if real, or expecting a virtual image to sit on a screen.

activities.title: Construct a plane-mirror diagram, normal first
steps: On paper (or a guided drawing tool), draw a mirror line and an incident ray arriving at it from an object point.
Before drawing any reflected ray, draw the dashed normal perpendicular to the mirror AT the exact point where the ray strikes.
Place the protractor centre on the point of incidence and measure the angle of incidence from the normal; record it to whole degrees.
Draw the reflected ray on the opposite side of the normal, measuring (not eyeballing) the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence.

Draw a SECOND incident ray from the same object point striking a different part of the mirror, draw its reflected ray the same way, then extend BOTH reflected rays' dashed back-extensions behind the mirror until they meet to locate the virtual image; label incident rays, normal, angle i, angle r, reflected rays, and image.
activities.insight: Both angles are measured from the normal, each reflection is symmetric about the normal, and the image behind a plane mirror is virtual — found where two reflected rays' dashed back-extensions meet, not where any real light travels.

activities.title: Refraction at an air→glass boundary and its exit
steps: Draw a rectangular glass block surrounded by air and an incident ray arriving at one face at an angle (not along the normal).
Draw the normal at the boundary and measure the angle of incidence from it.
Draw the ray inside the glass bending TOWARD the normal as a sharp change of direction at the boundary (not a curve).
Continue the ray to where it LEAVES the far side of the block and draw how it bends there, stating which way and why.
Label the normal (dashed), the incident, refracted and emergent rays (solid, with arrowheads).
activities.insight: Entering an optically denser medium at an angle, light slows and bends toward the normal; on leaving into air it bends away (for a parallel-sided block the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways). Refraction is a sharp change of direction exactly at the boundary, not a gradual curve; only a ray travelling along the normal passes through without bending.

activities.title: Locate a convex-lens image with principal rays
steps: Draw a convex lens with its principal axis and mark the focal points on each side.

Decide and mark where the object sits relative to the focal point, since this determines whether the image is real (object beyond F) or virtual (object between F and the lens); avoid placing it exactly at F, where the rays emerge parallel and no image forms.

Draw the known principal rays from the top of an object (e.g. the ray parallel to the axis that passes through the focal point beyond the lens, and the ray through the lens centre that continues undeviated).
Find where the rays (or their extensions) cross to locate the image point.
State whether the image is real (rays actually cross) or virtual (back-extensions cross), and label the diagram.
Note that only two rays are needed to locate an image point — choose the principal rays rather than guessing arbitrary rays.
activities.insight: An image is located where two chosen rays (or their extensions) intersect; a real image forms where light actually converges, and a virtual image where only the back-extensions appear to meet — for a convex lens, an object beyond F gives a real image, an object between F and the lens gives a virtual image, and an object exactly at F gives no image.

activities.title: Predict, then check against a real ray box
steps: Before using any apparatus, DRAW your predicted diagram for the chosen scenario (mirror, air→glass block, or lens).
Set up a ray box with a plane mirror, glass block or convex lens (whichever matches your predicted scenario) and shine a ray, or rays, to match your scenario.
Overlay or compare the real ray path with your prediction, marking where they agree and where they differ.
Reconcile any discrepancy: adjust your understanding or re-measure, and write down what caused the difference.
activities.insight: A ray diagram is a model that should predict the real phenomenon; comparing a prediction to observed rays exposes and corrects construction errors.

activities.title: Read and apply the drawing conventions
steps: Match each convention to its meaning: solid line = real light path; dashed line = normal or virtual/construction extension; arrowhead = direction light travels.
Given a diagram, identify which line should be dashed and from where the angle of reflection is measured (normal vs surface).
Re-ink or correct a diagram that uses one line style for everything so that real light paths and construction lines are visually distinct.
On a correct annotated exemplar, locate and explain each element (normal, angle i, angle r, incident/reflected/refracted ray, virtual image, arrowheads).
activities.insight: The conventions carry meaning: they distinguish real light from construction lines and show direction, so a diagram without them is an incomplete answer.

checkQuestion: Here is a half-finished ray diagram: a mirror line, a ray arriving at it, and a dotted line drawn at 90° to the mirror where the ray hits. First tell me what that dotted line is and what it's for. Then finish the diagram — draw the reflected ray correctly, and tell me which angles you'd put your protractor on to check it's right. Then, on this second diagram of a ray going from air into a glass block, draw how the ray continues inside the glass.
checkAnswer: The dotted line is the NORMAL — the line perpendicular to the surface at the point the ray strikes — and angles of incidence and reflection are both measured FROM it, not from the mirror. The reflected ray leaves on the other side of the normal with the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence (measured normal-to-ray on each side). Going into glass, the ray bends TOWARD the normal (it slows in the denser medium). Incident/reflected/refracted rays are drawn as solid lines with arrows; the normal and any 'image behind the mirror' construction lines are dashed.
